hints: Remember what an ideal gas assumes, that particles have no volume and no attractive forces between them.
Consider how high temperature gives particles lots of kinetic energy so attractions between them become insignificant.
Now think why low pressure, with particles far apart in a large volume, makes both particle size and attractions negligible.
walkthrough:
**Recall the ideal gas model**

An ideal gas assumes particles are point masses with no volume and no intermolecular forces. Real gases like nitrogen come closest to this when particles are far apart and moving fast.

Ideal gas equation:
$$pV = nRT$$

**Use high temperature**

High temperature means high average kinetic energy. Particles move so fast that any London dispersion forces cannot hold them together.

$$\text{high } T \rightarrow \text{high kinetic energy} \rightarrow \text{forces negligible}$$

**Use low pressure**

Low pressure means a large volume for the same moles, so particles are widely spaced. Their own volume is tiny compared to the container and collisions are less frequent.

$$\text{low } p \rightarrow \text{large separation} \rightarrow \text{most ideal}$$

**Pick the matching conditions**

Most ideal behaviour needs both effects together, high temperature and low pressure. That combination matches one row in the table.

options.A: Low temperature and high pressure is the worst combination. Cold particles move slowly so attractions matter, and high pressure squeezes them close so particle volume matters. This favours liquefaction, the opposite of ideal.
options.B: High temperature overcomes intermolecular attractions and low pressure keeps particles far apart. Both ideal gas assumptions are best satisfied, so nitrogen behaves most ideally here.
options.C: Low pressure helps, but low temperature hurts. Slow moving molecules at low T feel attractions more strongly and can even condense, so deviation from ideal is still large.
options.D: High temperature helps, but high pressure hurts. Squeezing the gas forces molecules close together so their finite size and attractions become significant, causing clear deviation from $pV = nRT$.
